comentarios.texto: Because `CryptoIntegration.init` is one-shot, calling `AuthzClient.create` first cements the global singleton with its own classloader and the minimal `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, so later server init is ignored and unsupported operations break. Guard the init in `AuthzClient.create` or avoid global init from the lightweight client.

hist.text: CryptoIntegration.init being one-shot is pre-existing; this PR makes detectProvider sort providers by order() (CryptoIntegration.java:56-57), with AuthzClientCryptoProvider at 100 and DefaultCryptoProvider at 200, so whenever the server providers are visible to the classloader they win. The 'minimal provider cemented' scenario needs a classloader split that no code here shows.

Creating AuthzClient first does not force its minimal provider: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:56-57 selects by descending priority, and DefaultCryptoProvider.java:83-84 assigns 200 versus AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:70-71's 100. Furthermore, quarkus/runtime/src/main/java/org/keycloak/quarkus/runtime/KeycloakRecorder.java:210-215 explicitly sets the server provider through CryptoIntegration.setProvider, which unconditionally replaces the singleton at common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:96-98, contradicting the claimed permanent lock-in.

Concede hallucination. The comment's load-bearing claim, that a later server init is ignored, is contradicted by the code: the Quarkus server installs its provider with CryptoIntegration.setProvider, which unconditionally replaces the singleton (KeycloakRecorder.java:214 `CryptoIntegration.setProvider(`; CryptoIntegration.java:96-98 `cryptoProvider = provider;`), and in a shared classloader detectProvider now picks the highest order() (`.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`, CryptoIntegration.java:56), so DefaultCryptoProvider (200) beats AuthzClientCryptoProvider (100). The described lock-in cannot happen.

comentarios.texto: Comparing an `_en` file against itself lets any anchor pass, so an unsafe anchor such as `javascript:` href is stripped before the sanitizer check and never reported. Skip anchor stripping when `file` is the English source or validate English anchors against the sanitizer policy.

hist.text: For an _en file, englishFile resolves to the same file (VerifyMessageProperties.java:77-78), so santizeAnchors strips every anchor before the sanitizer check. That is the intended model: the javadoc at line 147 says only anchors from the English source may appear in the translation, which makes the English source the trusted reference. Translations are still checked against it.

In misc/theme-verifier/src/main/java/org/keycloak/themeverifier/VerifyMessageProperties.java:74-86, an English resource loads itself as the reference, producing identical normalized values. Lines 150-155 therefore strip matching anchors, including javascript: hrefs, before the sanitizer runs at lines 88-92, so unsafe English anchors escape the newly added validation. This is a security weakness requiring an unsafe anchor in an English resource.

The facts are right (an _en file resolves englishFile to itself, VerifyMessageProperties.java:74-75, so santizeAnchors strips its anchors at :88), but that is the designed trust model, not a defect. The javadoc states the rule: `Allow only those anchor tags from the source key to also appear in the target key.` (:147-148). The English source is the reference the verifier checks translations against; the PR's purpose is sanitizing translated (community) resources, and translations still get every anchor matched against English (:153-158). Asking the verifier to also police the reference file is a feature request, not a regression this PR introduces. Severity as stated: a build-time verifier gap, not a runtime hole, so medium.

I change my classification to FP: the English resource is deliberately the anchor allowlist. VerifyMessageProperties.java:153–158 removes exact source-anchor matches and reports mismatches, so translations cannot introduce the claimed javascript: anchor unless it already exists in the trusted source. Self-comparison follows that policy; requiring independent validation of source anchors extends the verifier’s intended contract. Severity remains high assuming the alleged security weakness is true, as the rubric specifies.

comentarios.texto: A concurrent deleter racing between `SELECT` and `DELETE` leaves work remaining until the next cycle. Check `fetched` from `batchWork` instead of `affected` to decide when `untilDoneOrCancelled` is done.

hist.text: untilDoneOrCancelled stops when a batch reports 0 affected rows (xorm_store.go:650-654), and the batch returns deleteByIDs' RowsAffected. If another deleter removes the fetched IDs between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, the loop ends early. The only effect is that the remaining rows are cleaned on the next cycle, which the PR's own comment already accepts for concurrent inserts.

The PR separates the limited SELECT from DELETE at pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:529-538, returning RowsAffected from line 626; the loop exits when that count is zero at lines 656-657. A concurrent deletion through lines 423-430 can remove every selected row while other eligible rows remain outside the batch, causing cleanup to finish prematurely until the next cycle.

We agree the race exists (`if affected == 0 { return totalAffected, nil }`, xorm_store.go:656-657, with affected from `affected, err = res.RowsAffected()`, :626). The disagreement is whether it is worth a comment. It needs a concurrent deleter to remove every one of the fetched oldest IDs between fetchIDs (:530) and deleteByIDs (:536), and the only consequence is that remaining rows are deleted on the next cleanup cycle. The PR already accepts exactly that outcome as harmless: `This may under-delete ... any such annotations will simply be cleaned on the next cycle.` (:525). No user-visible effect, so nit / low.

I retain TP/medium: the new SELECT/DELETE split returns RowsAffected, and xorm_store.go:656 stops cleanup when that value is zero despite potentially remaining eligible rows. The bulk deletion path can remove every fetched ID between those statements. The concurrent-insert comment does not establish that abandoning an existing cleanup backlog is harmless; this race delays enforcement of configured retention limits. Recovery on the next cycle limits the impact, but this remains incorrect behavior under uncommon concurrency, matching medium rather than a nit.

Conceding. Applied strictly, the rubric's nit list (naming, style, docs, dead code, micro-optimisations, redundant work with no user effect) covers non-behavioural issues; this is a behavioural one. The loop exits on `if affected == 0 { return totalAffected, nil }` (xorm_store.go:656-657) where affected is deleteByIDs' `res.RowsAffected()` (:626), not len(ids) from fetchIDs (:530/:549). If a concurrent delete removes every fetched ID first, cleanup ends while eligible rows remain, so retention is not enforced until the next cycle. The PR comment at :525 only accepts under-deletion from concurrent inserts, not abandoning an existing backlog. The race is rare and recovers on its own, but it is still wrong behaviour on uncommon input: TP (no subclass), medium.

comentarios.texto: The background thread keeps calling `get_committable_offsets` and `commit_function` after rebalance/terminate with revoked partitions. After signaling `shutdown_event`, join `commit_thread` in `terminate` as `close` does.

hist.text: terminate() sets shutdown_event (queue_consumer.py:340-342), so _commit_loop exits after at most the iteration in progress; it does not keep committing. Any exception there is caught and logged. Not joining is consistent with terminate being the immediate, non-blocking shutdown, whereas close() is the graceful path that joins.

The newly added terminate() signals shutdown but never joins the commit thread (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:340-342). The loop does not recheck shutdown after wait(), so an in-flight iteration can retrieve offsets and call commit_function after terminate() returns and partitions are revoked (queue_consumer.py:274-287). It eventually exits, but the missing synchronization creates a real late-commit race.

Concede. I missed that the loop does not recheck shutdown after the wait: when terminate() sets the event, `self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0)` (queue_consumer.py:276) returns immediately and the same iteration still runs `get_committable_offsets()` and `self.commit_function(committable)` (:278, :287). terminate() (:340-342) neither joins the thread nor waits, so a commit can land after terminate returns and partitions are revoked, unlike close() which joins (:337). The file is new in this PR. Edge-case late commit, medium.

comentarios.texto: Model types with multiple underscores never match `ADMIN_MODELS` and get the wrong base path. Change `type.replace('_', '-')` to use `/_/g` so all underscores are replaced.

hist.text: basePath uses type.replace('_', '-') (rest.js.es6:22), which replaces only the first underscore. All current ADMIN_MODELS entries have at most one separator, including the new 'embeddable-host', so nothing misroutes today. It only matters for a future multi-underscore admin type.

app/assets/javascripts/discourse/adapters/rest.js.es6:1 lists only 'plugin', 'site-customization', and 'embeddable-host', so every supported admin model requires at most one underscore replacement. The single replacement at :22 therefore handles all entries correctly; using /_/g would not change routing for any configured admin model.

Concede FP. `const ADMIN_MODELS = ['plugin', 'site-customization', 'embeddable-host'];` (rest.js.es6:1) contains only entries with at most one separator, so `type.replace('_', '-')` (:22) routes every configured admin model correctly; no code path today hits a multi-underscore admin type. A latent issue with no reachable effect is FP (none), not a nit. Severity as stated (wrong base path for an uncommon type name) is medium.
